utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Good afternoon, ma'am. I beg your pardon. Good afternoon to everybody in and around the courtroom. Madam Registrar, will you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. This is case number IT-04-81-T, the Prosecutor versus Momcilo Perisic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much. Could we have the appearances starting with the Prosecution for today.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Dan Saxon for the Prosecution together with my colleagues Ms. Carolyn Edgerton and Bronagh McKenna and our case manager, Ms. Carmela Javier.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, and for the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Your Honours and everybody else in these proceedings. Novak Lukic and Gregor Guy-Smith for the accused.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I guess -- good afternoon, ma'am. May the witness please make the declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. You may be seated.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Is that you, Madam Edgerton?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: It is, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Good afternoon. You may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Good afternoon, and thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Witness.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MP-229
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: The first thing I'd like to do is have Madam Usher show you this piece of paper, and perhaps you could have a look at what's written on it and tell us whether that's your name and date of birth.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MP-229
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Madam Usher, could we then have that pseudonym sheet shown to my colleagues at the Defence table and then to Their Honours. Your Honours, could that please be marked as the -- as a Prosecution exhibit under seal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: That document is --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, Your Honour, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I beg your pardon. I'm sorry. The document is admitted into evidence. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be Exhibit P21 under seal, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Under seal, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, Witness, it's correct, isn't it, that you've given a total of five signed statements in regard to the incident on the 27th of February, 1995, two to police investigators and officials of your own country and three to the ICTY; is that so?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MP-229
utterances.text: Yes, yes, that is so.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Did you have an opportunity to review each of these in your own language before coming to testify today?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MP-229
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And did you have any additions, deletions, or alterations to make to these statements?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MP-229
utterances.text: No, I didn't.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, also before coming to court today, with my colleagues and with the assistance of an interpreter, did you review a copy of your testimony and cross-examination before this Tribunal when you appeared as a witness in the Dragomir Milosevic case?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MP-229
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And did you understand everything that you reviewed?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MP-229
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And if asked the same questions in respect of the incidents on the 27th of February today, would you give the same answers you gave in your previous statements and testimony?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MP-229
utterances.text: Yes, they would be the same answers.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Then, Your Honour, if I may, I'd like to provide the Chamber with the 65 ter numbers of the previous statements and testimony and documents referred to in the course of that testimony and ask that they be marked as exhibits.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: The first would be 65 ter number 09256; and as that's a signed statement, I'd ask that it be marked under seal -- or entered under seal. 09257, again, the same, under seal, please. 09258, again, under seal. 09259. I don't believe there's any requirement that that be entered under seal. 07186, 09260, 09261, and 092 -- sorry. Pardon me. 02708 should be the next number after 09261. And --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Yes, and I'm ably advised by my colleague Ms. Javier that 2708 has been already entered here as Prosecution Exhibit 19. And finally, Your Honours, the transcripts of the previous testimony 09262 and 09263.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: 65 ter number 09257 --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I'm so sorry. What's wrong today? 0926 -- 56 under seal, 09257 under seal, 09258 under seal, and then 09259, 07186, 09260, 09261, 09262, and 09263 are admitted into evidence. May they please be given exhibit numbers.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: 09256 will become Exhibit P22 under seal, Your Honours. 09257 will become Exhibit P23 under seal. 09258 will become Exhibit P24 under seal. 09259 will become Exhibit P25. 07186 will become Exhibit P26. 09260 will become Exhibit P27. 09261 will become Exhibit P28. 09262 will be Exhibit P29, and 09263 will Exhibit P30, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Your Honour, with your leave now, if I may, the -- those exhibits having been named, I'd like to read a brief summary of the evidence that's been tendered.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes. You may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. This witness, MP-229 will give evidence -- has given evidence in respect of scheduled incidents B10 and B11 of the indictment. This witness was born and raised in Sarajevo and in December 1994 became a tram driver. Around 12.15 on 27 February 1995, the witness was driving a crowded tram westwards along Zmaja od Bosne from the centre of Sarajevo to Ilidza. There was a cease-fire in place at the time, and there had been no combat activity near or around the tram on that day. When the tram was about 20 metres past the stop at the Marsal Tito Barracks, it came under a burst of gunfire from the left, which was an area exposed to Bosnian Serb -- I beg your pardon, which was exposed to the Bosnian Serb army-held area of Grbavica. This area was known to be dangerous. The witness heard people screaming and turned to see the passengers and blood on the floor. The witness continued to drive for about 50 metres, stopped where it was relatively safe, and opened the doors. Passengers got out in panic. MP-229 saw some that had been injured as a result of the shooting and also saw that the entire left side of the tram had been riddled with bullets. Scheduled incident B11 occurred four days later on March 3rd, 1995. MP-229 was driving a tram from the depot towards the centre of Sarajevo. When MP-229 approached Marsal Tito Barracks, the witness saw UNPROFOR soldiers signaling to drive on. When the tram MP-229 was driving reached safety, the witness stopped the tram behind three others and there was told by Slavica Livnjak that Livnjak's tram had been shot at. MP-229 went into Livnjak's tram and saw blood on the floor. After a while, forces from Grbavica started shooting at the trams. UNPROFOR soldiers returned fire, and the crossfire lasted for about 15 minutes. These experiences and the difficulties of living in Sarajevo generally had a major psychological impact on MP-229. That's the summary of the evidence of this witness, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And I have no questions of the witness, the evidence having been tendered.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you so much. Any cross-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have a few questions, Your Honours. Might I just be given a minute to prepare.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Madam Witness. I'm going to refer to you that way.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MP-229
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You've had court experience, and the two of us speak the same language. We understand each other, rather, so would you please make a pause between my question and your answer so that I can switch off my microphone and then you can continue. So just pause, count to three or four before you answer my questions. Thank you. We've just heard from that summary and introduction made by the Prosecutor that you testified in the Dragomir Milosevic trial. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MP-229
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: All of us here know that there was a first-instance judgement in the Milosevic trial, Dragomir Milosevic trial. So were you interested in learning what the judgement was?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MP-229
utterances.text: No. I didn't follow that.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I'm going to ask you to testify in the same way as you did in the Dragomir Milosevic trial, that is to say I'm going to show you a map, and I'm going to ask you about the different localities. But could you tell us just briefly what direction -- in what direction you were moving? Do you remember what tram stop you stopped before the tram was shot at? I think you said it was the Marsal Tito Barracks and so on. So just in a few words and then we'll take a look at the map.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The incident took place when I did my last round coming back from Carsija about 12.00, thereabouts; and when I started from the Marsal Tito Barracks stop, that's when the shooting started.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MP-229
utterances.text: Yes, that's right, from the centre towards the depot.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: So that's what you mean when you say Carsija?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MP-229
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You said in your statement, the one you gave to The Hague Tribunal -- that was your first statement, to be more precise. It was given in -- on the 13th of May -- no. On the 15th and 16th of November, 1995, is the date of that first statement of yours, and you said on that occasion that when you stopped at the Marsal Tito Barracks stop that you saw members of UNPROFOR there. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MP-229
utterances.text: No, I can't remember now.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: But anyway, you have had an opportunity, as you've just told the Prosecutor, to read through your statement a few days ago, and you found no reason to make any corrections, and you gave that statement in -- earlier on in 1995 when your memory was fresh.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MP-229
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. That was probably it.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Also in your statement, the one you gave to the Prosecutor in March 1996, you said that the source of the firing came from the Grbavica area to the left of you and that it was difficult to determine the source because people were shouting and screaming in the tram. That's what you said in that statement of yours. Do you remember?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MP-229
utterances.text: Well, I -- you didn't ask the question properly. I said that the shots came from my left-hand side. I didn't put it the way you said. I said that the shooting came from my left side.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: But you also said you -- that you didn't hear any shots and that you thought that the noise you heard was the wire above the tram, and then you turned to your right to look at the passengers, and then you realised, because when you testified in the Dragomir Milosevic trial you said that you weren't aware that it was actually shooting that had taken place.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MP-229
utterances.text: Well, that's right. There was shooting, something like that, but I didn't realise that they were bullets. And I turned to my right towards the passengers, and when I saw them falling down in the tram and I saw blood, then things were clearer to me. But at the first moment I thought that it was the wires breaking, the noise of the wires snapping above the tram.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Let me remind you. The Prosecutor just told us in the proofing session that you were shown your Milosevic testimony when Judge Robinson, the Presiding Judge at that trial, asked you how come you concluded that the shooting came from the direction of Grbavica. And on page 1622 you said -- your answer was, because the tram was hit on the left-hand side and that you knew that that was the area where the police forces were stationed. Do you remember saying that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MP-229
utterances.text: Well, yes, I do. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And you also said that you continued driving the tram for another 50 metres, roughly, to find a safe place to stop, and once you deemed it safe you stopped the tram.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MP-229
utterances.text: Yes, you're quite right. I continued driving the tram, but the tram just moved forward for as much as it could have because the -- the bullet was lodged in the front of the tram to my left where all the wiring and installations are. So in fact, the tram couldn't continue, so it -- the motion was through inertia and the energy it had beforehand.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'd now like to ask the usher to place the same map we used yesterday on our screens. I think it's 65 ter 448 or 4448. And can we zoom into the same area we were looking at yesterday, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And I'm just going to ask you to mark something on that map, but let's just wait to have the map put up on e-court.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we -- yes, fine. To the left a bit, and zoom in a bit more. Yes, that's fine.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Madam Witness, can you find your way around this map now?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MP-229
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, I can.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You'll be given a pen, and can you indicate with a line and an arrow the direction the tram was moving in and the Marsal Tito Barracks stop.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MP-229
utterances.text: Well, I can tell you the route I took, and it was this direction, from Carsija or the centre of town through Marin Dvor, and then the barracks were somewhere here in this area as far as I can see on the map.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I completely agree with you. I think that that's where the barracks were. So could you put a "B" there, please.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MP-229
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: For "barracks." And --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, six months down the line when you read that, will you be able to recognise that for a "B"? Can we get a "B" properly written maybe on the barracks themselves?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, indeed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Maybe a capital "B" might help.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Could you put a capital "B" at the spot where you thought the barracks were, a nice clear big "B." Take your time.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MP-229
utterances.text: Over here. That's as far as I can make out on this map.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: The Presiding Judge, Judge Moloto, doesn't think that we'll be able to read this when we come to look at this again later on, so perhaps you could place an "X" at that spot. That would be simpler, perhaps, an "X."

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MP-229
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Very well. Well, the usher will help us rub that out and mark it again. Just place an "X" where the tram stop was to make matters simpler.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MP-229
utterances.text: [Marks] I think you can see it now.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You said in your testimony that you noticed that something was happening and that you went on for some 20 metres. Now, could you mark the spot roughly where the shooting started and the spot where the tram was hit? And put a "1," if you can do that. If it's right next to the previous marking, then you don't have to.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MP-229
utterances.text: Well, I don't know why you want a number 1. It's right after I left the station. So perhaps I could mark it right next door. So if that was the tram stop, it might have been at that spot there or maybe even closer to the tram spot.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Well, it needn't be precise, just to give us a rough idea of what was happening and what things looked like. Now, can you draw in the locality where you think the forces who did the shooting and shot the projectiles at the tram were located. Could you circle that general area.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MP-229
utterances.text: It would be the Grbavica area, so to my left. I'm going to draw a circle around Grbavica like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And could you put a number 2 in the middle of that circle, please.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MP-229
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We've already heard testimony, and will you agree with me when I say that the Miljacka River was the separation line between the two territories, if I can put that way, one area covered by the BH army and the other area covered by the Republika Srpska in that part of town?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MP-229
utterances.text: Yes, that's right, in that part of town, but I don't know where the front lines were and things like that, where they had those lines, but that would be it generally.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And I'll ask you just one more thing. Could you please indicate on this map whether you know where the Vrbanja bridge is located and mark that with a number 3.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MP-229
utterances.text: I can't say exactly, but it should be approximately around here, in this area here. Somewhere around here, but I can't be precise.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I think you've done very well. It's actually written on the map but in very small letters. Could you please put a number 3 there. I think you're quite right. I think you've got the spot exactly.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MP-229
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, may this map be admitted into evidence?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: This map is admitted into evidence. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be Exhibit D2, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Tell me, please, after the moment when you turned round and you saw that the passengers were in an unusual situation, did you personally hear any shots after -- after that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MP-229
utterances.text: No, I didn't hear anything else except for the screaming of the passengers.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. May I ask you the following: First of all, would I be correct in saying that that was the only tram line functioning in Sarajevo at the time, this route along the Zmaja od Bosne Street?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MP-229
utterances.text: Yes. I don't know how familiar you are with Sarajevo, but that was the only line. That's the only route the trams took.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We heard some testimony -- or, rather, I read some testimony, and you may know more about this, about when the tram started running in Sarajevo. You told us, actually, but do you know when it began?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MP-229
utterances.text: I can't remember precisely, but it was about two or three months before we began our training and before we were received into the service, but I really don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Tell me, at that time how long was your daily shift?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MP-229
utterances.text: About four or five rounds. I was in the first shift in the morning, so it would be from around 5 a.m. to about 12.30 or 1 p.m..

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: That was the morning shift, but was there an afternoon shift as well?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MP-229
utterances.text: Yes, there was a second shift, as well, but it would all depend on the situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: So there were two shifts from morning to afternoon? Am I right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MP-229
utterances.text: Yes, yes. There was the first and the second shift.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: From what my learned friend has read out, we heard that a few days later, on the 3rd of March, you were in the tram again when you were a witness to the second event when the tram in front of you was attacked. This was some five days later if I remember correctly.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MP-229
utterances.text: Yes. I continued working, and it happened again, the same incident, but it was another tram that was hit this time.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Madam Witness, in your testimony in the Milosevic case, on pages 1638, you stated that the Serb side did not respect the cease-fire. Will you agree with me that the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina also failed to respect the cease-fire, and do you know something about UNPROFOR protesting about their failure to respect the cease-fire in that period?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MP-229
utterances.text: I don't know about that, but I do know about the Serbian army because I was involved in these unfortunate incidents.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Are you aware that the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina in late 1994 and in 1995 was considerably better equipped with weapons, that they also had snipers? Do you know something about that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MP-229
utterances.text: Believe me, I really don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Would you agree with me if I said that part of Grbavica was also under the control of the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MP-229
utterances.text: To the best of my knowledge, this part there was not under their control. I'm not sure exactly where the lines were, but I know which areas we could not pass through, which areas were out of bounds.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: In your testimony in the Milosevic case, Dragomir Milosevic, page 1623, answering a question by the Prosecutor, you said you did not remember on the day when there was an incident involving your tram whether there were any army of Bosnia-Herzegovina soldiers on your tram.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MP-229
utterances.text: No. I remember them asking me whether there were any soldiers, and I said that there happened to be a soldier next to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: That's what I was going to ask you because I read that in your statement to the police, but it isn't clear from your testimony before the court. So you said that after the incident when the tram was inspected you saw a soldier of the army of Bosnia and Herzegovina on the tram and that you knew him from before because he had worked in the same company as you. Is that how it was?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MP-229
utterances.text: No. What I said was that the soldier was standing next to me, and we started chatting as I was driving, and it turn out that we had been colleagues, that he had been working in the same company as me, but I didn't know him from before.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Well, in any case, we have the statement on record. So he was a soldier of the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina, and he was traveling on the tram and talking to you in the course of the ride?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MP-229
utterances.text: Well, I suppose he was a soldier because he was wearing an army of Bosnia-Herzegovina uniform, but how would I know?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You also said that you thought that a cable had snapped, but I'll put the question more precisely, although I can anticipate your answer. Before and after that, you didn't hear any other shooting in the area?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MP-229
utterances.text: No. It was very quiet that day. There was no shooting or anything else happening, at least in the town itself. I don't know what was going on in the vicinity of the town.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You didn't hear that there had been a clash on the bridge at Vrbanja?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MP-229
utterances.text: No. I was doing my job, and had there been something happening someone would probably have told us, informed us about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I have one more question about this incident. You said in your testimony that when the tram was inspected afterwards, 30 bullets were found in the tram -- or rather, in the body of the tram and the glass, but we have information that eight or nine bullets were found. Could I be right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MP-229
utterances.text: Well, you could be because I didn't count the bullets. I only saw that it went in a zigzag line. When I got out at the depot, I went out -- I got off the tram to take a look, but it was a burst of fire in a kind of zigzag line. That's what I remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: With respect to the second incident, I have only one question. You said that you heard that a tram which a colleague of yours was driving, Ms. Livnjak who was in front of you, do you remember how many trams were standing there? Was her tram the first? Were there other trams there? Can you recall?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MP-229
utterances.text: Yes, I do recall that. I didn't hear the shooting. I was the second or the third tram in the line, but to the best of my recollection Slavica was on that side, and then there may have been two other trams between us, and mine was the third. And then I heard the shooting, and then you know about the S-curve in Sarajevo, and then I went on. There were one or two trams in front, and it was then that I stopped, and it was only when I got out and came closer that I saw something was wrong, and Slavica told me there had been shooting, and I saw blood.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have no further questions for this witness, Your Honours. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Lukic. Any re-examination, Madam Edgerton?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: No, Your Honours. However, I would ask your indulgence if we could go into private session. I've noticed some -- two occasions where I'd like to raise an issue with respect to a small redaction, two occasions on the transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Aren't we in closed is session? No. Okay. May we go into private session, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we're back in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Mr. Saxon, I saw you rising.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I simply rose to indicate to the Chamber that the Prosecution has no more witnesses available today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you very much. In that event, I guess we'll adjourn to tomorrow at quarter past 2.00 in the afternoon, same courtroom. Court adjourned.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Sorry. Sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Subject to the appeal judgement being delivered, yes. As soon as it ends, we'll start, and the court is ready. Thank you very much, so I can't give time. Court adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
